questions.stem: Which of the following is quantitative data?
options: A photograph of a damaged delivery
The number of units sold per store per week
questions.explanation: Quantitative data is numerical, measurable and countable, and answers how many / how much / how often. A, C and D are qualitative — descriptive of qualities or characteristics.

questions.stem: A dataset records each store's postcode as a four-digit number. What level of measurement is postcode?
questions.explanation: Nominal — A postcode is a label, not a quantity — averaging postcodes produces a meaningless number. The exam trap is assuming digits imply quantitative data. Test: does arithmetic on it mean anything?

questions.stem: Temperature in degrees Celsius is an example of which level of measurement?
questions.explanation: Interval — It has order and equal intervals, but zero is arbitrary (0 °C does not mean "no temperature"). This is why 20 °C is not "twice as hot" as 10 °C — ratios are invalid. Kelvin, by contrast, is ratio because 0 K is a true zero.

questions.stem: Which statistic is the most appropriate measure of centre for Likert-scale responses?
questions.explanation: Median — Likert data is ordinal — ordered but with unequal intervals — so the mean assumes a precision the data does not have. Mode and median are valid; mean and SD are not.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to know why checkout abandonment rose. Which approach is best?
options: Increase the sample size of the existing dataset
Collect qualitative data through exit surveys and user interviews
Convert existing data to ratio level
questions.explanation: Quantitative data tells you what is happening (abandonment is 42%); qualitative tells you why (shipping cost appears too late). A mixed-methods answer is the strongest exam response.

questions.stem: In the DIKW model, what distinguishes information from data?
options: Information has been processed, organised and given context
Information is stored in a database
questions.explanation: Data is raw, unprocessed facts with no context. Information is data processed, organised and contextualised so it has meaning. Knowledge then applies information to make decisions; wisdom applies judgement.

questions.stem: Informatics is best defined as:
options: The process of turning data into information and knowledge to support decisions
questions.explanation: Informatics is the transformation of data → information → knowledge → wisdom to support decision-making, and includes the people, processes and technology that make that transformation happen.

questions.stem: Which is an example of semi-structured data?
options: A JSON file returned by a weather API
A relational database table of sales records
questions.explanation: JSON has tags and markers giving it some organisation, but no rigid predefined schema. A is structured; C and D are unstructured.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of enterprise data is typically unstructured, and why does this matter?
options: A small minority — it is easily queried with SQL
Exactly half — it is stored in data marts
The large majority — it requires ML or NLP techniques rather than SQL to analyse
None — all enterprise data is structured
questions.explanation: The bulk of enterprise data is unstructured (email, documents, images, video, audio, social posts). It cannot be queried with conventional SQL, so it needs NLP, computer vision or ML — which is a major driver of data-lake architectures and AI adoption.

questions.stem: A number that identifies a player's jersey is best classified as:
options: Nominal, because it functions as a label
Interval, because the numbers are ordered
Ordinal, because higher numbers indicate seniority
questions.explanation: Nominal — The digit is an identifier only. No arithmetic on it is meaningful — jersey 10 plus jersey 4 is not jersey 14.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly describes CCTV footage captured automatically for security?
questions.explanation: Computerised because a system captures it without an operator; passive because the subject does not knowingly engage in the collection.

questions.stem: The main advantage of active data collection over passive collection is:
options: It produces far larger volumes of data
It captures data in real time
Participants consent and can explain their reasoning, giving context
questions.explanation: Active collection (surveys, interviews) is consented and contextual — it can capture why. Its costs are the opposite: slow, expensive, small samples and vulnerable to response bias.

questions.stem: A researcher splits a population into age brackets and samples proportionally from each. This is:
questions.explanation: Stratified — The population is divided into strata (subgroups) and sampled in proportion, guaranteeing each subgroup is represented — critical when subgroups behave differently.

questions.stem: A quality-control officer tests every 50th item off the production line. This is:
questions.explanation: Systematic — Every nth record is selected. It is simple and cheap, but risks periodic bias if the production cycle happens to align with the sampling interval.

questions.stem: The greatest weakness of convenience sampling is:
options: It requires a complete sampling frame
The sample is unlikely to represent the population
questions.explanation: Sampling whoever is easiest to reach systematically excludes people who are harder to reach, producing selection bias. It is fast and cheap, which is exactly why it keeps being used badly.

questions.stem: In RAVR, validity asks:
options: Is the data related to the question?
Is the data close to the true value?
Is the data measuring what it claims to measure?
Would repeating the method give consistent results?
questions.explanation: Validity = measuring the right construct. (A) is relevance, (B) is accuracy, (D) is reliability. A bathroom scale that reads 2 kg heavy every time is reliable but not accurate.

questions.stem: A set of scales consistently reads 3 kg too high. The data is:
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of the method; accuracy is closeness to the true value. A systematic offset is perfectly repeatable and perfectly wrong.

questions.stem: An operator types 1243 instead of 1234. This is a:
questions.explanation: Transposition — Characters have been swapped. A transcription error is a general mistyping. Check digits are specifically designed to catch transpositions.

questions.stem: Which validation check would prevent a date of birth of 2099-01-01 from being accepted?
questions.explanation: Range check — It confirms the value falls within acceptable limits. A type check would only confirm it's a date; a format check only that the pattern is YYYY-MM-DD.

questions.stem: The distinction between validation and verification of data entry is:
options: Validation is manual; verification is automated
Validation checks reasonableness at entry; verification checks the data was transferred/entered correctly
Validation happens after storage; verification before
questions.explanation: Validation = "is this sensible and correctly formed?" (range, type, presence, format, check digit). Verification = "is this what was on the source?" (double entry, proofreading). Validated data can still be wrong.

questions.stem: An outlier in a dataset should first be:
options: Investigated to determine whether it is an error or a genuine extreme
questions.explanation: Deleting outliers without investigation destroys real signal — fraud, equipment failure and your best customer all look like outliers. Any treatment applied must be documented and justified.

questions.stem: Which is an example of response bias?
options: A model trained on unrepresentative data
Survey respondents overstating how often they exercise
A sensor drifting out of calibration
Only sampling customers who visit the website
questions.explanation: Response bias is participants answering what looks good rather than the truth (also called social-desirability bias). (A) is algorithmic bias, (C) measurement bias, (D) selection bias.

questions.stem: An enterprise trains a recruitment model on ten years of its own hiring decisions, which favoured one demographic. The model replicates that pattern. This is:
options: Algorithmic bias arising from biased training data
questions.explanation: The model has learned and now automates historical discrimination, applying it at scale with a veneer of objectivity. Mitigations: representative data, bias auditing, fairness metrics, diverse teams and ongoing monitoring.

questions.stem: Which is metadata rather than data?
options: The text of a customer review
The date and time the review was submitted
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data — author, timestamp, file size, geotag, schema, device. Note that metadata alone is often enough to identify and profile a person, which is why it is privacy-relevant.

questions.stem: A dataset contains the same customer twice under slightly different name spellings. The most appropriate treatment is:
options: Leave both records to preserve completeness
Convert the names to nominal codes
Deduplicate via fuzzy matching during the data cleaning stage
questions.explanation: Duplicate records inflate counts, distort averages and break customer-level analysis. Data cleaning (cleansing/scrubbing) handles duplicates, missing values, inconsistent formats and impossible values.

questions.stem: Secondary data's most significant limitation is that:
options: The collection methodology was set by someone else and cannot be verified
It is always out of date
It is more expensive than primary data
questions.explanation: You inherit someone else's sample, definitions and instrument. It may be perfectly good data for a different question. Its advantages are speed, cost and scale.

questions.stem: Sampling is used instead of a census primarily because:
options: A census is often too costly, slow or impractical
Samples do not require ethics approval
questions.explanation: A well-designed sample trades a known, quantifiable margin of error for enormous savings in time and cost. It does not eliminate bias — poor sampling creates it.

questions.stem: Which sampling method carries the highest sampling error for a given sample size?
questions.explanation: Cluster — Because whole naturally occurring groups are sampled, members within a cluster tend to be similar, so effective information per observation is lower. It is chosen for cost and logistics, not precision.

questions.stem: A survey is distributed only through the enterprise's mobile app. The resulting dataset most likely suffers from:
questions.explanation: App-only distribution systematically excludes non-users — often older, lower-income or less digitally connected customers — so the sample cannot represent the whole customer base.

questions.stem: "Garbage in, garbage out" in a data science context means:
options: Storage costs rise with poor data
Data must be deleted after use
Analysis and models can be no better than the quality of the input data
questions.explanation: No amount of sophisticated modelling repairs biased, inaccurate or unrepresentative input. This is why cleaning and RAVR assessment precede analysis, not follow it.

questions.stem: What makes a blockchain tamper-evident?
options: Each block is encrypted with the user's private key
Blocks are stored on a single secure server
Each block stores the hash of the previous block
questions.explanation: Altering a block changes its hash, so the next block's stored "previous hash" no longer matches — and the break cascades forward through every subsequent block. Rewriting history requires recomputing all later blocks and out-computing network consensus.

questions.stem: A hash is best described as:
options: A reversible encryption of a block
A digital signature issued by a bank
A fixed-length one-way fingerprint of the input data
questions.explanation: One-way and fixed-length: any change to the input, however small, produces a completely different hash. You cannot recover the input from the hash.

questions.stem: A smart contract is:
options: A legally binding paper agreement stored digitally
Self-executing code on a blockchain that runs when specified conditions are met
questions.explanation: Because it executes automatically and is recorded immutably, it removes the need for an intermediary — but a bug in the contract is also immutable, which is a genuine enterprise risk.

questions.stem: In a blockchain, a node is:
options: The hash of the previous block
A participant computer holding a copy of the ledger
questions.explanation: Distribution across many nodes is what makes the ledger decentralised — there is no single point of failure or single party who can quietly rewrite it.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants tamper-evident, auditable provenance records for its coffee supply chain. Blockchain is appropriate mainly because:
options: It provides a shared immutable record no single participant can retrospectively alter
It processes transactions faster than a database
It removes the need to collect data
questions.explanation: The value case is trust between parties who don't fully trust each other. Where a single trusted party controls the data, a conventional database is cheaper and faster — that's the limitation to name in an evaluate question.

questions.stem: A consensus mechanism exists to:
options: Allow nodes to agree that a block is valid before it is added
questions.explanation: Examples include proof of work and proof of stake. It is what prevents any one node from unilaterally adding fraudulent blocks — and, in the case of proof of work, what makes blockchain energy-intensive.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine limitation of blockchain for enterprise use?
options: High energy use, low transaction throughput and the difficulty of correcting an erroneous entry
Data cannot be shared between organisations
questions.explanation: Immutability cuts both ways: a wrong entry can only be superseded, not erased — which collides with the right to erasure under GDPR-style privacy law.

questions.stem: The "three Vs" of big data are:
questions.explanation: Volume, Variety, Velocity — with Veracity (trustworthiness) and Value (usefulness) commonly added as a fourth and fifth.

questions.stem: A retailer processes point-of-sale, clickstream and sensor data as it arrives, in real time. This is a challenge of:
questions.explanation: Velocity — the speed of generation and required processing. The infrastructure implication is stream processing rather than overnight batch, enabling in-the-moment decisions like blocking a fraudulent transaction mid-authorisation.

questions.stem: A data warehouse differs from an operational database because it is:
options: Smaller and normalised for fast writes
Integrated, cleaned, historical and structured for analysis
questions.explanation: The warehouse is the analysis layer: subject-oriented, integrated from many sources, time-variant and non-volatile. The operational database (OLTP) is optimised for many small fast transactions instead.

questions.stem: In ETL, the Transform step involves:
options: Writing the data into the warehouse
Cleaning, standardising, deduplicating and aggregating the data
questions.explanation: Transform is where "NSW", "N.S.W." and "New South Wales" become one value, units are reconciled and business rules are applied. It is also where invisible editorial decisions get baked in.

questions.stem: A data lake without governance becomes a:
questions.explanation: Data swamp — raw data accumulated without catalogue, metadata, quality standards or ownership, so nobody can find or trust anything in it.

questions.stem: A data mart is best described as:
options: A marketplace where enterprises buy datasets
A raw store of unprocessed data
A subject-specific subset of a data warehouse serving one department
questions.explanation: For example, a marketing data mart drawn from the enterprise warehouse. Benefits: faster queries, simpler models, departmental control. Risk: marts drifting into conflicting definitions of the same measure.

questions.stem: A supermarket discovers that customers who buy nappies frequently also buy a particular snack. This is:
questions.explanation: Association rules find items that co-occur. It informs product placement, bundling and recommendations — but co-occurrence is not causation, and low-support rules are often noise.

questions.stem: Segmenting customers into previously unknown groups based on behaviour, without predefined labels, is:
questions.explanation: Clustering — an unsupervised technique. Classification differs because it assigns records to known, predefined categories using labelled training data.

questions.stem: A bank flags a transaction that deviates sharply from a customer's normal pattern. The data mining technique is:
questions.explanation: Anomaly detection — Its enterprise trade-off is the false positive: freezing a legitimate customer's card is a real cost, so the detection threshold is a business decision, not just a technical one.

questions.stem: Predicting a numeric value such as next quarter's revenue from historical variables uses:
questions.explanation: Regression — modelling a numeric relationship to predict a continuous value. Classification would predict a category (churn / no churn) instead.

questions.stem: Data mining is best defined as:
options: Discovering previously unknown patterns and relationships in large datasets
questions.explanation: The emphasis is on previously unknown — running a report you already designed is querying, not mining.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest ethical objection to data mining of customer purchase histories?
options: It can infer sensitive attributes such as pregnancy, illness or financial stress that the customer never disclosed
questions.explanation: Inference sidesteps consent entirely — the customer consented to record purchases, not to have a health condition deduced. This is the core of the "secondary use" problem in privacy law.

questions.stem: An enterprise keeps raw sensor data for 7 days and hourly aggregates for 5 years. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Tiered retention — It balances analytical value against storage cost, and supports the privacy principle of not retaining personal data longer than necessary.

questions.stem: A foreign key is:
options: A field that uniquely identifies each record in its own table
A field that references the primary key of another table
Two fields combined to form a unique identifier
questions.explanation: The foreign key is what physically creates the relationship between tables. (A) describes a primary key and (C) a composite key.

questions.stem: A student can enrol in many subjects and each subject has many students. To implement this in a relational database you need:
options: A junction table with a composite primary key
questions.explanation: A relational database cannot store M:N directly. The junction (link/bridge) table — e.g. ENROLMENT — resolves it into two 1:M relationships and gives attributes of the relationship itself (Grade, DateEnrolled) somewhere to live.

questions.stem: Referential integrity requires that:
options: Every table has a primary key
All fields are validated on entry
Every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value
questions.explanation: It prevents "orphan" records — an order pointing at a customer who does not exist. Enforced by the DBMS through cascade or restrict rules on delete and update.

questions.stem: Normalisation primarily aims to:
questions.explanation: The trade-off is that heavily normalised schemas require more joins, which is exactly why analytical warehouses are deliberately denormalised (star schemas) for query speed.

questions.stem: Which SQL clause filters rows before aggregation?
questions.explanation: WHERE — HAVING filters after GROUP BY has aggregated. Classic exam distinction: WHERE amount > 100 filters individual rows; HAVING SUM(amount) > 100 filters groups.

questions.stem: SELECT Suburb, COUNT() FROM Customer GROUP BY Suburb ORDER BY COUNT() DESC; returns:
options: An error, because COUNT cannot be used with GROUP BY
One row containing the total customer count
The number of customers in each suburb, most populous suburb first
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per suburb, COUNT(*) counts members of each group, and ORDER BY ... DESC sorts largest first.

questions.stem: Which SQL operation combines rows from two tables based on a matching key?
questions.explanation: JOIN — UNION stacks result sets vertically (same columns); JOIN widens rows horizontally by matching a key.

questions.stem: In crow's foot notation, the "crow's foot" symbol at one end of a relationship line indicates:
questions.explanation: Many — A single perpendicular bar means one; a circle means optional (zero); combinations read as "one and only one", "zero or many", etc.

questions.stem: A flat file system's core weakness compared to a relational database is:
options: Data redundancy leading to inconsistency and update anomalies
questions.explanation: The same customer's address repeated across a thousand rows means one address change requires a thousand correct edits — and any missed row makes the file internally contradictory.

questions.stem: A DBMS provides all of the following except:
options: Guaranteed accuracy of the data entered
questions.explanation: A DBMS enforces structural correctness — type, range, referential integrity — but cannot know that a correctly formatted address is the wrong address. Validation is not truth.

questions.stem: In a spreadsheet, =VLOOKUP(A2, Products!A:C, 3, FALSE) returns:
options: The third column value from the Products table for an exact match on A2
The nearest approximate match in column 3
An error, because FALSE is invalid
questions.explanation: The final FALSE forces an exact match, which is almost always what you want — TRUE (approximate) silently returns wrong values on unsorted data and is a common source of quiet spreadsheet errors.

questions.stem: A pivot table is most useful for:
options: Rapidly summarising and cross-tabulating large datasets by category
questions.explanation: It aggregates (sum, count, average) across chosen row and column dimensions and lets you re-orient the summary instantly — essentially OLAP-style analysis inside a spreadsheet.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet feature works backwards from a desired result to find the required input?
questions.explanation: Goal Seek — "What unit price gives me $200,000 profit?" Scenario Manager and Data Tables extend this into multi-variable what-if analysis.

questions.stem: A composite key is used when:
options: The table has more than 10 fields
No single field uniquely identifies a record
questions.explanation: For example, in an ENROLMENT table neither StudentID nor SubjectID alone is unique, but the combination is.

questions.stem: In a data dictionary, which of the following would you expect to find?
options: Field name, data type, size, format, validation rule and description
The visualisations produced from the data
The names of all system users
questions.explanation: The data dictionary documents the meaning and rules of each field, so a maintainer years later knows what CUST_STAT_3 actually holds.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The primary advantage of cloud storage over on-premises storage for a growing enterprise is:
options: Absolute control over the physical hardware
Elastic scalability with pay-as-you-go cost and no capital outlay
Guaranteed compliance with all privacy laws
questions.explanation: The counterweights are ongoing subscription cost, dependence on connectivity, vendor lock-in and data sovereignty exposure — which is what (C) and (D) get wrong.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Data sovereignty means:
options: Enterprises own all data they collect
Governments may access all cloud data
Data is subject to the laws of the country in which it is physically stored
questions.explanation: So Australian health data stored on US servers may be reachable under foreign law regardless of Australian contractual promises — the reason many public-sector tenders mandate onshore hosting.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Under the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, an enterprise must:
options: Publicly publish the full breach dataset
Notify affected individuals and the OAIC of eligible breaches likely to cause serious harm
questions.explanation: The trigger is an eligible data breach likely to result in serious harm. Notification must be prompt, and both affected individuals and the OAIC must be told.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: How many Australian Privacy Principles are there under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth)?
questions.explanation: 13 APPs — , covering open and transparent management, collection, use and disclosure, direct marketing, cross-border disclosure, data quality, security, and access and correction.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Since 10 June 2025, Australians have had a new legal avenue in privacy: the statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy. Its significance for enterprises is that:
options: Only the OAIC can bring an action
Individuals can sue directly, including against entities not covered by the APPs
It replaces the Privacy Act entirely
It applies only to government agencies
questions.explanation: The tort covers intrusion upon seclusion and misuse of information, and reaches parties beyond APP entities — so a small business or individual can be liable even where the Privacy Act would not apply.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: From 10 December 2026, Australian privacy policies must disclose:
options: The physical address of all servers
The use of automated decision-making that significantly affects individuals' rights or interests
questions.explanation: ADM transparency obligations force enterprises to say, in their privacy policy, where computers are making consequential decisions about people — directly relevant to credit scoring, recruitment screening and insurance pricing.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: De-identification reduces but does not eliminate privacy risk because:
options: Individuals can sometimes be re-identified by combining the dataset with other data
questions.explanation: Re-identification through linkage attacks is well documented — a few quasi-identifiers (postcode, birth date, sex) are often enough. Hence suppression of small cells and aggregation before publication.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The CARE principles for Indigenous data governance stand for:
options: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, Ethics
questions.explanation: CARE is people-and-purpose oriented and complements the technically oriented FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). Related: ICIP — Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Which best describes the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: Three backups taken every two days by one person
Three-year retention, two-year archive, one-year deletion
Three encryption keys, two administrators, one vault
Three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy offsite
questions.explanation: Modern practice adds an immutable or air-gapped copy specifically to survive ransomware, plus restore testing — an untested backup is not a backup.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: In the CIA triad, integrity means:
options: Only authorised people can read the data
Data is accurate, complete and has not been improperly altered
questions.explanation: Confidentiality = who can see it, Integrity = is it unaltered and correct, Availability = can you get it when you need it. Ransomware attacks availability and integrity.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Which is a supervised machine learning task?
options: Grouping customers into segments with no predefined labels
Predicting whether an email is spam using a labelled training set
Reducing the dimensionality of a dataset
An agent learning through trial-and-error rewards
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labelled examples to predict a known output. (A) is unsupervised, (D) is reinforcement learning.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: The purpose of holding back a test set is to:
options: Increase the size of the training data
Measure performance on data the model has never seen
questions.explanation: Evaluating on training data measures memorisation, not generalisation. The validation set tunes hyperparameters; the test set is touched once, at the end.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: A model performs excellently on training data and poorly on new data. This is:
questions.explanation: Overfitting — the model has learned noise specific to the training set. Remedies: more/better data, simpler models, regularisation and cross-validation.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Reinforcement learning is characterised by:
options: Training on a fully labelled dataset
An agent learning a policy through rewards and penalties from its environment
questions.explanation: Used for robotics, game playing, dynamic pricing and logistics routing — problems where the right action is only revealed by consequences over time.

questions.topic: Storage, security, law and machine learning
questions.stem: Over time, a deployed model's accuracy degrades because customer behaviour has changed. This is:
questions.explanation: Drift — The world moved and the model didn't. It is why deployed models need ongoing monitoring and scheduled retraining — an ML system is an operating commitment, not a one-off build.

questions.stem: A logistics enterprise stores GPS telemetry from 800 trucks at one reading per second. Which is the most defensible design decision?
options: Store every reading indefinitely in the operational database
Filter and aggregate at the edge, transmit exceptions and hourly summaries, tier the retention
Discard all telemetry after each trip
Store the data unencrypted to speed up analysis
questions.explanation: It addresses velocity and volume simultaneously, cuts bandwidth and storage cost, and aligns with the privacy obligation to collect and retain only what is necessary. (A) creates cost and privacy exposure; (C) destroys analytical value; (D) is indefensible.

questions.stem: A hospital's dataset shows a strong correlation between ice-cream sales and drowning incidents. The correct interpretation is:
options: The correlation proves seasonality is irrelevant
The data must contain transposition errors
A confounding variable — hot weather — plausibly drives both
questions.explanation: Correlation is not causation. Always test whether a confounding variable explains both, whether the relationship is plausible mechanistically, and whether reverse causation is possible.

questions.stem: An enterprise's marketing and finance teams report different values for "active customers". The most likely root cause is:
options: Inconsistent business definitions applied in separate data sources or marts
questions.explanation: This is the "one version of the truth" problem. The fix is a governed warehouse with conformed dimensions and a documented, agreed definition of each measure — a governance issue, not a technical one.

questions.stem: A dataset of 50,000 records has 38% missing values in the "income" field. The most defensible action is:
options: Delete the field and note the limitation, or impute with a documented method and report the effect
Fill the blanks with the maximum observed value
Ignore the issue and report the mean of the remaining records without comment
questions.explanation: Zero-filling (B) fabricates poverty; (C) fabricates wealth; (D) hides a probable non-random missingness pattern. Whatever you choose, state which and why — undocumented imputation is the real failure.

questions.stem: A supermarket claims its loyalty data proves customers prefer its own brand. The strongest methodological criticism is:
options: Loyalty data captures only members' in-store purchases, excluding non-members and competitors' baskets
The data is stored in a warehouse
questions.explanation: The sampling frame is the enterprise's own loyal customers — the population most predisposed to agree with the conclusion. It cannot support a claim about customers generally.

questions.stem: Which statement about metadata retention is correct in a privacy context?
options: Metadata is not personal information and carries no privacy obligations
Metadata such as location, timestamps and contacts can be highly identifying and revealing
Metadata is exempt from the NDB scheme
questions.explanation: Who you called, when, from where, and how often can reveal more than the call's content. Metadata is squarely within privacy regulation when it relates to an identifiable individual.

questions.stem: An enterprise migrating to a data warehouse should perform which check after loading?
options: Compare record counts and control totals between source and target
questions.explanation: Row counts, checksums and control totals on key measures are the standard reconciliation. Silent partial loads are one of the most common and most damaging migration failures.

questions.stem: Which is the best justification for using a relational database rather than a spreadsheet for a growing booking system?
options: The database enforces integrity, supports concurrent multi-user access and scales beyond spreadsheet row limits
questions.explanation: Concurrency, referential integrity, validation, access control and scale are the structural advantages. Spreadsheets remain excellent for small, single-user, exploratory analysis.

questions.stem: In an evaluation of a data collection method, which piece of evidence would most strengthen a claim of reliability?
options: Repeating the same instrument on the same population produced consistent results
questions.explanation: Reliability = consistency on repetition (test–retest, inter-rater agreement, internal consistency). Size, security and convenient conclusions say nothing about it.

questions.stem: An enterprise uses AI to screen job applications. Under Australia's Guidance for AI Adoption, the most important governance control is:
options: Increasing training data volume without review
Human oversight of consequential decisions plus impact assessment and transparency
questions.explanation: The six practices are governance and accountability, impact assessment, risk management, transparency, testing and monitoring, and human oversight — with recruitment a paradigm high-impact use case.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest example of secondary use of personal data?
options: Using a delivery address to deliver the order
Using purchase history collected for order fulfilment to build a health-risk profile sold to a third party
questions.explanation: Data collected for one purpose is reused for a different, unconsented purpose. APP 6 restricts use and disclosure to the primary purpose or a reasonably expected related purpose.

questions.stem: A data analyst chooses to display the median rather than the mean household income. This is most defensible because:
options: Income distributions are right-skewed, so the mean is pulled upward by high earners
The median is easier to calculate
The mean is invalid for ratio data
questions.explanation: With skewed distributions the median better represents the typical case. Reporting both, plus the distribution, is the fullest answer.

questions.stem: An enterprise is deciding between OLTP and OLAP infrastructure for a new executive reporting system. The correct choice and reason is:
options: OLAP, because it is optimised for complex historical, aggregated queries across dimensions
OLTP, because it handles many small transactions
Neither — a flat file is sufficient
questions.explanation: OLTP runs the business (fast small writes, normalised, current); OLAP analyses the business (few very large reads, denormalised, historical, multidimensional).

questions.stem: Which action best protects data integrity during collection from a web form?
options: Storing entries as free text with no constraints
Applying validation rules — presence, type, range, format and check digits — at the point of entry
questions.explanation: Preventing bad data at entry is far cheaper than detecting and correcting it later. Encryption protects confidentiality, not correctness.

questions.stem: A start-up wants to analyse customer sentiment from 200,000 free-text reviews. The most appropriate approach is:
options: Natural language processing with sentiment classification, validated against a human-coded sample
A pivot table on the review text
Converting the reviews to ratio data
questions.explanation: NLP scales to unstructured text; validating against a human-coded subset is what makes the output defensible rather than merely plausible.

questions.stem: An enterprise argues it does not need consent because its data is "publicly available on social media". The strongest counter-argument is:
options: Public availability does not remove privacy obligations — collection, use and disclosure of personal information still engage the APPs, and aggregation can create new sensitive inferences
Public data cannot be stored in the cloud
questions.explanation: "It was public" is not a legal or ethical defence for scraping, profiling or re-purposing. Scale and aggregation change the nature of the intrusion.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a data cleaning process was well conducted?
options: A documented, repeatable log of every rule applied, records affected and justification, with the raw data preserved unchanged
questions.explanation: Reproducibility and an untouched raw copy are the hallmarks. (C) is confirmation bias dressed as validation.

questions.stem: For a small retailer, the strongest argument against adopting a full data warehouse is:
options: Warehouses are illegal for small business
Warehouses cannot connect to visualisation tools
Build cost, ETL complexity and maintenance overhead exceed the analytical benefit at that data volume
questions.explanation: Right-sizing the solution is a genuine EC-12-08 judgement: a well-structured relational database plus a BI tool may deliver 90% of the value at 10% of the cost.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders the analytics pipeline?
options: Collect → clean/transform → store → analyse → visualise → decide
questions.explanation: Note the pipeline is iterative — discovering a quality problem at the analysis stage sends you back to collection, not forward to visualisation.

questions.stem: An enterprise claims its ML model is "objective because it removes human judgement". The best critique is:
options: Human judgement is embedded in the choice of training data, features, labels and success metric — the model automates those judgements rather than removing them
Models are always less accurate than humans
Objectivity is guaranteed by large datasets
questions.explanation: Every model encodes a chain of human decisions. The danger is that automation launders those judgements into apparent neutrality and applies them at scale.
